speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thought that after the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) had heard the persuasive speeches of members of the NDP, it would not be necessary for me to make this speech. But the jolly green giant of the cabinet apparently is not persuaded at this stage, and therefore it is necessary for me to make my speech. In all the speeches that have been made during this debate, and in the discussions that have taken place across the country, there has been one common trend throughout; that is, agreement that Canada is in its worst period of inflation, recession and unemployment since World War II.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

speechtext: And bad government.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I think this is the reason we have to address ourselves to this problem, which is not only a national problem but an international one. When you think of the low inflation we had in the 1960s, 1 per cent to 1.5 per cent, and the high inflation we are having in the 1970s, 11 per cent to 12 per cent, the enormity of the problem becomes clear.
With regard to recession, we have not been able to gear our productive capaticy to a point where we are meeting the needs, demands and expectations of most Canadians, and therefore we are in a recession period. We are also in the highest unemployment period that Canada has experienced. I notice that one of the Ottawa members nods his head. I thought he was going to say it is even higher than during the Conservative regime form 1958 to 1962.
At the end of September we had a seasonly adjusted unemployment figure of 732,000, indicating a 7.2 per cent rate. When you look at the distribution of the unemployment rate, you find that in the province of Newfoundland it is 18.8 per cent; in New Brunswick it is 10.4 per cent; in Quebec, 9.3 per cent; and in British Columbia, 9.6 per cent. This underlines the problem of unemployment across the country. If there is anything that the former minister of
Anti-Inflation Act
finance bequeathed to the present Minister of Finance, it is that today we have the highest unemployment ever, the highest food prices, the highest interest rate and the highest rate of inflation.
Hon. members may recall that when the former minister of finance resigned, the question in the minds of many Canadians was who would replace him. Now we have the present Minister of Finance. His was an unexpected appointment, for most Canadians, although I might say it was probably a good appointment when we consider the other cabinet material which was available. The Minister of Finance has come forward with his own and the cabinet's solution to the problems of inflation, recession and unemployment. We in the New Democratic Party have said that his response to these problems is both unfair and unworkable. We have said that it will not build any new houses, it will not provide reasonable food costs, it will not combat the shrinking purchasing power of those on fixed incomes, it will not increase production, and it will not put Canadians back to work.
There have been many analytical reasons put forward as to why we have inflation, but I think we are all agreed that ours is not the traditional supply and demand type of inflation. It was rather interesting to glance at Walter Gordon's book in which he says that inflation today is not caused by the marketplace machinery, but by monopolies which set the price of most consumer goods. In his recent book "Storm Signals" he sets forth his reasons for saying that Canadian consumer prices are set by monopolies which operate in the marketplace. They are not concerning themselves with the problems of supply and demand but, instead, with the demand for their particular products, and setting prices not in relation to the cost factor but in relation to their administered prices of which profit is the foremost factor.
I was interested in what Mr. Gordon said with regard to the monopolistic companies which control the Canadian economy. I will list a few of them to indicate the strength of his reasoning. The petroleum field is not controlled by Canadian companies but by monopolistic foreign companies. The companies are Imperial Oil, Gulf Canada, Shell Canada, Texaco Canada, and BP Canada. When it comes to mining, again there is monopolistic control by companies outside Canada which operate the firms of International Nickel, Falconbridge Nickel, Noranda Mines, Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting, and Rio Algom.
With regard to forest products, again we have monopolistic companies the ownership of which is outside Canada. Those companies are Canadian International Paper, Abitibi and its subsidiary, Price Company, MacMillan Bloedel, and Crown Zellerbach, Canada. We know that the automobile industry is controlled by General Motors of Canada, Ford, Chrysler and American Motors. With regard to computers, there is IBM. When it comes to aluminum, there is Alcan Aluminum. The liquor industry is controlled by Seagrams, Hiram Walker, Godderham, and so on. Beer is controlled by Labatt's, Molson's, Carling and O'Keefe. With regard to tobacco, we have IMASCO, MacDonald's Tobacco and Rothmans. That is just a short list of the control which monopolistic companies have with regard to consumer products which Canadians must

October 24, 1975
Anti-Inflation Act
have to enjoy a certain quality of life, and this indicates the problem the government is facing in controlling these multinational companies.
I usually analyse the shortcomings of a bill before giving the New Democratic Party remedies to the problem, but this time I will reverse the order and give the remedies of my party to the problems of inflation, recession and unemployment. I will capsulize them for reasons of time, and I hope for the persuasion of hon. members. The first remedy of the New Democratic Party would be to impose selective action to stop unnecessary price increases. The first prices all of us can think of would be oil and gas. We would pass legislation rescinding the 10-cent excise tax on gasoline. With regard to the oil and gas industry, the zooming profits of recent years should be brought to the attention of hon. members. With regard to Imperial Oil, Gulf Canada and Shell Canada, there are figures available on their profits and their percentage of return.
In the years 1970 to 1974, Imperial Oil had a net income increase of 176 per cent and a rate of return of 22 per cent. Gulf Canada had an increase of net income, in the years 1970 to 1974, of 313 per cent and a rate of return up to 20 per cent. Shell Canada had an increase of net income from 1970 to 1974 of 178 per cent and a rate of return of 16 per cent. These figures indicate the necessity of controlling oil and gas companies across the country. Their profits are unconscionable and the government has done little or nothing to stem that tide. I might say that this bill will do little or nothing to control the rate of return of oil and gas companies.
This pattern applies across the board and includes financial institutions and the large corporations which operate in Canada. Recent figures for banks have shown very sharp increases in profits in the past few years. The same is true for large corporations. Therefore, to combat this problem we would set up a prices control board with power to investigate and roll back increases which are not justified.
The second approach would be this. We would make sure that the impact of inflation on those who suffer the most from its effects would be cushioned. I am speaking of people on low incomes and fixed incomes. We would increase old age pensions and veterans allowances so that the recipients could meet some of the high costs they are experiencing today. It is not sufficient to say that a cost of living increase is part of their pension. What is necessary is a pension which is adequate to meet the demands of the day.
The federal government should give leadership by amending the Minimum Wages Act. This would benefit people on low incomes in that they would have sufficient money to provide necessities for their families. Over and above that, there are people who have personal hardships. We must devise programs which will meet these personal hardships. With the extra money they would have, we could increase the demand for goods and services, which would have the effect of helping the unemployment problem and also the problem of production.
Our third method of solving the problems of inflation, recession and unemployment, would be to have a massive housing program. I am looking forward to the programs the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) now

has on the drawing board. I hope he will bring them forward very soon. The programs he has brought forth have had a little effect but not a substantial effect on this problem. In the final analysis I think the federal government has to give the initiative and leadership to parliament to control housing and earnings across the country. We have suggested that the government should increase its allotment of money for land assembly and direct construction and, more directly, with regard to the control of mortgage rates.
Neither in Bill C-73 nor more especially in the white paper has the government taken the real initiative with regard to controlling interest rates. It has stated that it will let them fluctuate because of the international demands for money.
I hope that I can persuade the Minister of Finance that there are three types of interest. There are consumer loans which have a particular rate of interest, business loans which have a particular rate of interest, and mortgage loans which have a particular rate of interest, and they are all different. There is no reason why the government cannot direct the financial institutions to set aside a certain allocation of their investment moneys for housing at a particular, low interest rate. This is a social responsibility and it is up to the government to direct the financial institutions to take this action.
We have said that the interest rate should be fixed at 6 per cent. Of course 6 per cent would operate to the detriment of the profit and loss statement of the banks, but it is absolutely necessary if we are to combat the high cost of housing and high rents that prevail. There is a certain persuasion in the suggestion of the members of the Conservative party that an income tax allowance be made concerning the high interest rate after a maximum of 8 per cent, but in the ultimate analysis if we are going to talk about a reduction in the cost of housing we have to strike the main components, land and interest. Interest is the most flagrant abuse of the profit power. Therefore I think the government has to take the initiative. I am rather disappointed that the white paper did not spell out the necessity of controlling interest rates at a moderate figure.
Those are the three main approaches that the New Democratic Party would take on these vital problems, Madam Speaker. My colleagues have done an excellent job of analysing the shortcomings of Bill C-73. I would only remind the House that the Liberal response to inflation was set forth by the Minister of Finance, who said that we must distribute the burden equally across Canada. This is an attempt to perpetrate a cruel hoax on Canadians. The minister knows that the weight falls heavily on people with low incomes.
When I was younger I remember reading the works of George Bernard Shaw. He said there is one thing about rich people, they will do anything except get off the backs of the poor. I think it is the same today-they will do anything except get off the backs or out of the pockets of the ordinary working people.
The philosophy of the minister's approach is wrong. He comes from the riding adjacent to mine so we have many things in common. There are working people, and people
October 24, 1975

of many different ethnic origins, who are attempting to develop a quality of life of which they can be proud. He and I have a certain consensus on what should be done regarding housing and so forth, so I hope he will take note of what we are saying and take some action. But I see no sign of it in this bill and I am not the only one who cannot see it.
When I see the minister's approach to profits, limiting them to 90 per cent of the average net pre-tax profits over the preceding five years with special exemption for export products, then I look at the oil companies-Imperial, 176 per cent in the last five years; Gulf, 313 per cent; and Shell 178 per cent. They will continue to enjoy the high prices and profits they have enjoyed in the last few years; they have the strength, the power, the corporate sleight of hand to protect themselves fully. This also applies to banks and large corporations. There are too many exemptions, too many loopholes with regard to the profits of corporations across the country.
It has been announced that wages will be restricted to an 8 per cent increase in the first year 6 per cent in the second year, and 4 per cent in the third year, with a minimum of $600 and a maximum of $2,400. I am sure most Canadians feel this should be reversed so that people on low incomes should get $2,400 and people on high incomes should get $600.
I notice the new Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) is in the House. I want to congratulate him on his appointment; it is an excellent one. I believe he is a man of competence, ability, and compassion. I would hope he will find a way to reverse that approach of $2,400 for people on high incomes and $600 for people on low incomes. How can people even get the $600 if they do not belong to a union? How can people on low incomes attempt to get it? What bargaining power do they have? And what about pensioners, what about veterans? There is no assurance that the Minister of Finance is going to make a statement that these people will get the minimum of $600.
We have had a statement about rents. Following the meeting of the provincial ministers of finance the Ontario treasurer, Darcy McKeough, stated that the Ontario government is going to wait to impose rent controls. I am sure that the Minister of Finance wants the Ontario government to move, and move quickly, because there are many people within his riding, and all Ontario ridings who have been directly affected by high rents. I hope he will take his usual strong, tough, attitude which he displays at times, and tell the Ontario treasurer that his approach is not good enough and that these measures must be taken immediately to give protection to the people of Ontario in regard to high rents.
Finally, Madam Speaker, I should like to refer to the board itself. It is a very difficult and cumbersome board to operate. I am sure the chairman and its members are going to encounter real difficulties in regard to appeal board procedure, going to the Federal Court and then to the cabinet. This just means it will be cumbersome and complicated, and cause delays. It does not give me confidence that it can solve our problems.
In conclusion, Madam Speaker, from the Prime Minister's statement one could take it that it is possible that changes will take place. I suppose this is as a result of his dialogue and the speeches he has made across the country.
Anti-Inflation Act
Most of his speeches have been made to high income groups. Every time he goes to a meeting where trade unions are involved he is rejected.
Speeches which members of the New Democratic, Conservative, and Creditiste parties have made across the country will, no doubt, influence the Prime Minister, to make changes. But I can just hear what he will say-"We will increase the minimum exemption for wage earners from $600 to $800, and we will not impose heavy restrictions on dividends, as the corporations are exerting pressure." Really, that is not good enough. I hope the Minister of Finance will not adopt a sphinx-like attitude and say, "That is all we can do now; when times are better we shall make changes." He may suggest amending the Income Tax Act just before the next election in order to help people. I hope that will not be his attitude. I hope he will take positive initiatives and will not do some of the things he suggested he may do. As I say, I hope he adopts some of the remedies the NDP has mentioned. I say that because I am sure all Canadians agree that only by working together can we make this a better country, a country where all Canadians can live a better life.
Members of the NDP, in common with many Canadians, feel that Bill C-73 will not be adequate for dealing with the problems of inflation, recession, and unemployment. That is why we will not hesitate to vote against this bill as it stands. We hope the minister will introduce changes which will incorporate some of our ideas, and thus make this a better country in which to live.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that it was appropriate for this bill to be introduced by the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald), the Minister of Finance, as I think it reflects the thinking of people who are fortunate enough to live in affluent parts of the country, like Rosedale.
I am not from Rosedale, Mr. Speaker, and I want to bring to the government's attention the thinking and concerns of people who are not lucky enough to live in affluent places like Rosedale or Mount Royal. I shall take my examples from the north, but what I am about to say will apply equally to the Maritimes or the east end of Vancouver. In those areas few will need to worry about the government's ceiling of $2,400 on raises. Not many people in those areas make that kind of money.
The average income of most working families in the Northwest Territories, my part of the country, is around $8,000 per year. Most of us are used to the idea of buying gasoline at a high price. The average price of gas in my part of the country is just about $1 per gallon. It is not at all unusual to pay $1 for a quart of milk. So you might say that we knew about inflation long before the word became fashionable in Montreal or Toronto. Therefore, when I talk to the government about these problems, I sometimes feel tempted to charge consultant's fees.
We in the north have spent a lot of money learning about inflation and should be given special consideration, possibly in the form of special tax concessions. For instance, people who live north of the sixtieth parallel should be allowed special allowances. These might induce more physicians to practice in the area. I suggest that

October 24, 1975
Anti-Inflation Act
there should be more adequate recognition of conditions in the high Arctic, especially economic conditions which are not the same as in the rest of the country.
The government has created many of our economic difficulties. It has proposed wage and profit controls as a solution to these difficulties. In its wisdom the government has lumped all our economic problems under the catchword inflation. It has said that we should now knock the wind out of inflation, and it proposes to attack inflation by controlling our wages.
What is the government doing to solve other problems like unemployment, monopolistic market structures, and in housing and transportation? Housing and transportation, particularly, are important matters for my constituents, as well as for many others in this country.
Over and over again you hear members of this House talking about the problems in housing and problems in transportation. I tell them that transportation is one of the big problems in my area. The high cost of transportation has led to the very high cost of living with which people must cope in the part of the country I represent. Even though the government refuses to acknowledge these problems, I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that they exist. The white paper which preceded this legislation touched, at one point, on these problems. It is too bad that the concern shown was not translated into legislation. The part to which I refer was near the beginning of the white paper, in that section dealing with the infrastructure of our economy.
The job market is one of the structures of our economy. What is happening in the job market? The national rate of unemployment is over 7 per cent; in some parts of the country it is over 20 per cent. Statistics show that the unemployment rate for native people in northern Alberta is about 65 per cent. I guess unemployment is not much of a problem in constituencies like Rosedale or Mount Royal.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
What about the housing problem? One can see many problems in the housing part of our economy. Housing costs take a big chunk out of peoples' take home pay, and the percentage lately has been getting bigger, faster. I suggest that these increased costs have nothing to do with the wage demands of a tin bash or of a swamper. No, Mr. Speaker, high costs have much to do with high mortgage rates.
In Yellowknife a house costs almost twice as much as a comparable house costs in Edmonton, although the two centres are only 1,000 miles apart. In Rankin Inlet, in the Northwest Territories, the problem is even worse. People who do not have a government job cannot buy, rent, steal, or borrow a house. I guess hon. members opposite and to my right would explain this in capitalist terms by saying that in Rankin Inlet there is a seller's market. Anyone who manages to put up a small, poorly insulated house in Rankin Inlet could ask for the price of the moon as rent, and get it. That will show you how bad things are in Rankin Inlet. As I said, we in the Northwest Territories know about inflation. That is why I say this bill will do little or nothing to solve the problems I mentioned, problems existing in my part of the country.

Transportation is another part of our economic infrastructure. Hon. members may be surprised to learn that the Northwest Territories are served with bus lines. The bus provides a cheap link between Edmonton and Yellowknife. It moves people and goods cheaply between those two centres. Actually, most of us in the north depend on air transportation, although merchants use the bus system to ship small items from the south. The price of shipping by bus recently rose by 30 per cent. As the increase took place on October 1, this legislation will not roll it back. That 30 per cent price increase will be borne by people like Jerry Rieman who runs the camera store in Yellowknife. Jerry will pass the increase on to his customers, and they will pay it. We shall see increases in the cost of aviation fuel, and other increases in transportation costs. We know they are coming. This legislation will permit them and they will be passed on to the consumer. Those increases will be inflationary. This bill will do nothing to stop them.
This bill does not stop the inflation problems of the ordinary consumer. It does stop the inflation problem of those who live in places like Mount Royal and Rosedale. What is that problem? The problem is trying to stop paying more and more for wages. People who live in places such as Rosedale and Mount Royal are more likely to be employers than employees.
The government has solved one inflation problem for a few people. However, when prices go up because of higher transportation costs, higher housing costs, or anything else that will fit through a loophole in this bill, other people will pay. They will pay for it out of take home pay that has been frozen, frozen because the elected representatives from Rosedale and Mount Royal think that controlling wages is the only answer to inflation in our economy. As I said, some people in other parts of the country do not agree with them.
I am sure some members opposite are about ready to tell me that the price controls outlined in the bill will stop inflationary price increases. Before they do that, let us look at what will happen when the price of gas will again go up.
Pacific Western Airlines, which operates out of British Columbia and Alberta into the western Arctic, will be forced to increase its rates on merchandise being shipped to a wholesaler in Yellowknife. That wholesaler will have to raise his price on goods going to Snowdrift, Fort Simpson, or wherever. Retail outlets in these places will have to raise their prices and the consumer will have to pay the increase out of his controlled wages. That is just a simple example.
Into the picture comes the Anti-Inflation Board. Let us say they get there three or four months after the initial increase and their investigation goes on for a month. After that time they may decide the airline was not justified in increasing its freight rates. Is the board going to see to it that the consumers in smaller communities, who for months have been paying five or ten cents more for items will be reimbursed? I seriously doubt that.
The board will not be able to stop all the other five and ten cent increases that are bound to occur, not even if they had 5,000 employees instead of 500. They will not be able to do that because this bill only stops increases in wages.
October 24, 1975

To sum up, I wish to emphasize that the inflation problems of most Canadians are not solved by this bill. They are caused by a limited supply of housing, trends on the international commodity markets, and the concentration of market power in the hands of fewer and fewer corporations. These problems are also caused by the inability of the government to show any economic leadership.
I hope that the leaders of the business community who live in places like Rosedale and Mount Royal are happy with their elected representatives. I know that people in many other parts of the country, especially those in the Northwest Territories, are not happy with such members.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I start on the substance of my report I wish to refer to the hon. member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth) who on half a dozen occasions chose to refer to my constituency as being particularly affluent, and indicated that therefore I would bring to this question a rather narrow viewpoint. I think it is unfair to put to the hon. member for Northwest Territories the requirement that he know in detail all aspects of the country. He has a lot of ground to cover himself.
I can understand that the hon. member might not know my constituency very well. But he obviously was not listening to his colleague the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert), who spoke just five minutes before, pointing out how similar his electorate was to mine, that is Broadview and Rosedale. I am going to say about the characterization that if I am a fat cat, I guess the hon. member for Broadview is as well.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
The hon. member for Northwest Territories does not have to listen to me or visit my constituency, but he should listen to the hon. member for Broadview. He is a man of excellent spirit and sentiment, even if from time to time I disagree with some of his judgments.
In reply, I would like to state that since I last had an opportunity to participate at second reading I have discussed the white paper and Bill C-73 with the provincial governments in the two-day federal-provincial meeting. I wish to refer briefly to that meeting and also to some of the points made during the debate.
With regard to the federal-provincial meeting, the provinces really agreed on three essential points. First, they agreed with our expression of concern about the current economic situation, in particular with regard to the trend in the rates of inflation as requiring special action; second, that the initiative for this action must appropriately and properly be taken at the federal level and by this government; third, that while there may be certain details of the program we put forward with which they disagree, and upon which they would like to see changes-as I said in question period today, we will certainly consider changes and I will refer to those in a moment-in general they are
Anti-Inflation Act
prepared to support and co-operate with these particular proposals.
One of the points that emerged at that meeting and which should be pointed out in this debate is that a policy with regard to prices and incomes, by definition cannot possibly deal with all of the economic issues in Canada. There are many serious questions with which we have to be concerned. The question of regional disparity has been referred to by a number of my colleagues on this side. There is also the question of range of incomes within the community in a vertical sense, and the kinds of changes we should have particularly when dealing with those on fixed income.
The first point is that we cannot and should not by this policy alone try to overcome the problem of regional disparity. We should continue to try to improve the policies that have been and are being followed by my colleagues in that area. On the other hand, we should not by this program seek to make the disparity any worse. It is for that reason I have to reject, for example, the suggestion of the treasurer of Ontario that there should be cuts in the DREE program. This is a question which has also been raised in the House.
With regard to government expenditures, obviously there will have to be some hard decisions taken in connection with the 1976-77 estimates. There will have to be some cuts which will be painful in certain parts of the country. However, with regard to certain policies, Regional Economic Expansion is one we should seek to make more efficient, but we should certainly not make it a particular victim of our inflationary concern.
The second point is that over the years there have grown into our economy and society inequalities in incomes. Some of these have come about directly as a result of collective bargaining. Under our system the trade unions have been in a position to bargain for more favourable treatment, not only to create difference as between different worker groups in our community, but within the structure of a union itself, a scale of compensations. So one cannot hope to overcome by a prices and income program alone differences in economic return to various people in Canada.
Governments in Canada essentially over the years have assumed responsibility for providing basic standards of income for the unorganized, for example through the minimum wage laws both at federal and provincial levels. As I had an opportunity to say in this House yesterday, my colleague, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro), had the opportunity yesterday afternoon to continue the federal-provincial discussion of the minimum wage in Canada.
It is a fair observation that in the past there has been a certain ambivalence among the various provinces in regard to this matter. On the one hand there is the very legitimate concern of people elected in public life to try to divert their efforts specifically at those at the bottom of the income scale. There has been the equal concern often expressed at these meetings that a too rapid increase by the federal government will put pressures on those in certain of the provinces who are not under federal jurisdiction. My colleague will be in a position to report on

October 24, 1975
Anti-Inflation Act
these discussions in due course, but the question of the minimum wages is one that has been covered during the last 24 hours at the federal-provincial meeting.
In addition to that, as I have said to the Leader of the New Democratic Party, under the old age security plan, the guranteed income supplement, the Canada Assistance Plan, and now under the new and more recent provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act we have provided for other groups in our community that are not in a position through economic power or through collective bargaining to take care of themselves.
After all of these speeches in this debate are in, however, the basic problem will still remain, and that is the one with which I started off the debate, namely that if those with economic power can obtain higher and higher levels of compensation, then there are two inevitable results. In the first place, given that the quantity of additional resources in Canada is finite, there will be less and less available for those who are without economic power. Secondly, higher returns for those in a position of economic power, whether you talk about doctors or lawyers, corporate executives or public servants, steel workers or auto workers, landlords or corporations-those increases have to be paid for by somebody in the community. They are in fact paid for by everybody. They become a net cost increase for all of us in the community. When that occurs and they become a net cost increase, they therefore, in part at least, become the responsibility of those at the bottom of the income scale, among others, to have to pay.
It seems to me that those basic facts are ones that we as a nation have to come to terms with in this proposal. As I said in opening, we are not going to join in the argument about whether or not the wage increases and catch up increases of the past are responsible for inflation. We are insisting, however, that if all major groups with power insist on big increases, or on leap frogging ahead for the future, in the long run there will be a net cost for all of us to pay which will have to be passed on, and in due course it will be borne by the economy and will result in another inflationary increase.
During the course of the federal-provincial conference a number of problem areas arose, and I will refer briefly to them. Reference was made this afternoon to rents. May I say in fairness to the provincial treasurer of Ontario that he was not averse to taking early action on rents. However, he did accede to representations made by other provinces that the provinces as a whole should proceed together on the basis of national criteria. The fear, of course, was that if there are different regimes from province to province, this could have an adverse comparative effect with regard to investment in new accommodation. In fairness to Mr. McKeough, he was not the dilatory person in this particular discussion. I think it can be said that no one was. But there was a basic problem of trying to get some national standards followed by each of the provincial governments in carrying forward this part of the price control program which will be carried out under provincial jurisdiction.
The second point that was difficult and which has been much raised in this debate, for example by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) last night, is

that of professional income. This is one of tl-*s most difficult of the questions that were raised. I do not think that anyone would claim that those of professional income who, relatively speaking in terms of numbers, are not a substantial percentage of the work force, are alone responsible for dramatic increases in incomes. Rather there is the comparative problem that if they do not seem to be covered by this program then the program looks unfair. It would want that quality of equity in which all appear to share in restraint.
In this discussion we recognized a lot of the frailties put forward by the hon. member. I think, without coming to any final conclusion on this, that there was a recognition yesterday that possibly there would have to be in the first place, between the federal and provincial governments- particularly with the provincial government participation since the concept of a self-governing profession is established under provincial law-some agreement on appropriate fee schedules, and possibly, to reinforce this question and the equity of the matter, a surtax might have to be considered and perhaps imposed at the federal level.
With regard to the medical profession-not the profession of the hon. member for New Westminster or my own-we recognized that in some ways we would be working against some of our other objectives in public policy if we were too restrictive in terms of what we did. If we said that there would be limits on income from the existing level of effort but that for additional hours put in, or additional patients seen, there could be a further increment, we would run into financial problems, to say nothing of a health and safety problem with a practitioner who sees half as many patients again as he saw last year, which would likely mean he would not do as good a job for his patients as he should.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext: In case of lawyers it would be good if they stopped working.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Additional work for lawyers would seem to suggest that there would be a rampant crime wave in this country, but I will be objective enough not to wish that upon the country in the interests of my own profession.
The third element that was much discussed in this debate, one that has been discussed in the Liberal caucus and was very effectively referred to by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Joyal), the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), and the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. McRae), is the appropriate maximum level for those at the lower end of the income scale, the $600 limit. It appears both from the federal-provincial meetings and from the debate here that there is some consensus that the $600 limit is not appropriate. What is lacking, however, is consensus on an appropriate alternative method. On behalf of the government obviously I will have to pursue this question with my colleague to see whether we can find some satisfaction in this respect, particularly in light of minimum wage discussions.
As for prices, it has been asserted long and repeatedly that there is no way that prices can be effectively monitored and controlled.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Or accurately controlled.
October 24, 1975

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Yes, accurately controlled. The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) feels that in my new character I should not get involved in debate and I am trying to reform, but may I remind him again very gently of what I said on second reading, namely, that those in the group he now leads did not always think it was impossible to control prices.
I think it is fair to point out that many prices can be controlled in advance. Indeed, the chairman of the AntiInflation Board has set about doing just that by requiring notification in advance of a price increase, and by requiring justification before any price goes up. That is the kind of regime that we had over the past two years with regard to petroleum pricing in Canada at the crude level. With regard to certain other products, particularly with consumer durables, automobiles, household goods, white goods and goods of that kind, the cost factor is such that it is reasonable to expect that justification will be required first.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext: Is that going to be the case in respect of automobiles?

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
The price justification in that particular case would present no difficulty, and I think that should be done. I see no difficulty in doing that, nor with regard to certain services such as those covered by bank charges, once again there seems to be no effective argument against requiring justification in advance for that kind of change.
On the other hand, a real problem arises in a sector that affects every family in Canada every week, and that is, of course, with regard to the marketing of food products through the supermarkets. In this regard, as I have said elsewhere, it is not possible to have a policeman behind every bottle of marmalade, so there will be difficulties involved in the change of basic food prices from week to week. It will be very hard to have this kind of justification. We would try to control that in respect of gross profit margins by applying the same kind of test that this industry applies to itself for its own purposes.
Finally, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) in his speech said the banking and financial institutions would not be dealt with in this measure, but I would point out that they will be dealt with and in fact are covered in the white paper, and I include the insurance companies and chartered banks. The same cost pass through formula I just mentioned a moment ago would apply to them, therefore they would be restricted in respect of their increases in rates in the same way.
Before taking my seat, Madam Speaker, there were several questions of a legal nature raised which I should like to deal with now if I may. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) raised a question as to whether the Canadian Bill of Rights would apply to this particular bill. The answer is that indeed it would as there is no provision in here exempting the application of the Canadian Bill of Rights. Indeed, it is because of the obligation under that Bill of Rights not to deprive a person of property or liberty without due process of law that the formula covering,
Anti-Inflation Act
first, the appellate review, and then a judicial review of the work of the administrator is provided under this particular bill.
The question was raised at several points, by the hon. member for Peace River and by the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), as to whether it would be proper at some interval before the termination date of the bill to provide for a fresh parliamentary opportunity, perhaps by way of an affirmative resolution, to debate the matter. For my part I would have no difficulty in accepting an amendment of that kind.
Having regard to the reports, I would think one of the essential elements of the work of the Anti-Inflation Board would be that there should be an extensive public report of its findings, and I am sure the board and the chairman will seek to do that. In addition to those reports there is a provision in the bill that reports from the administrator are to be made from time to time to the minister, and they are to be put before parliament. In conclusion. Madam Speaker, that deals with some of the broader questions on the implications of the program.
A number of serious questions as to detail were raised. I would be pleased to attend with legal counsel at the committee proceedings to discuss these questions. I have in mind the constitutional question raised by the hon. member for Greenwood. I would be prepared to discuss some of the other legal questions raised by hon. members, particularly the one raised by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave). I agree it would be desirable to have other officials, in addition to legal ones, on the financial side appear to answer questions both as to the bill and as to the concept of its administration.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to assure my colleagues, especially the Parliamentary Secretary to the House leader, that he does not have to take a pill, I will be brief and his bill will be passed shortly.
However, I would like to take this opportunity to repeat what some of my colleagues and I have already said during the consideration of the bill in committee. We pointed out to the President of Treasury Board, mainly responsible for the introduction and passage of that bill that in our opinion, he did not go far enough as far as the pensions of Lieutenant Governors are concerned.
In committee, we tried to convince the President of the Treasury Board to change the text of the bill itself to take into account the particularly difficult circumstances under which the lieutenant governors of Quebec and their families took over the functions they now assume.
But the bureaucrats won that inning and, unfortunately, the President of the Treasury Board refused to follow the advice shared by most of the members of the committee. He won. But I am giving him another chance, and urge him to reconsider his position, Madam Speaker, because of the unfairness of the situation. Of course, I am speaking in relative terms with regard to the lieutenant governor of New Brunswick who fills his post, in some regards, at his own expense. He has to dig in his pockets to pay some of the expenses incurred in the course of his duties, duties which he has to perform and which he is expected to perform in view of his position.
I should have been remiss in my duty had I not pointed this out today. I know that several of my colleagues from New Brunswick on the other side support the stand we have taken, and I think it is most unfortunate that the procedure should not allow us to amend the bill as we would have wished with regard to the lieutenant governors of New Brunswick and Quebec.
One of my colleagues may wish to add to what I have said. That is why, Madam Speaker, I now bring my remarks to a close.

subtopic: SUGGESTED ROYAL COMMISSION STUDY TO IMPROVE SAFETY OF PASSENGERS AND EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I seem to be once more on familiar grounds, or should I say familiar rails, in rising to speak again on this motion brought before the House by the hon. member for Rimouski. I am very much aware of the deep concern expressed by my worthy friend, but again I must answer him as I did last October 28 when he brought the matter before the House in practically the same words.
This matter of railway safety which the hon. member has brought up for discussion, continues to be a principal concern of the government, particularly as rail transportation received strong emphasis in the new transportation policy tabled in the House last June. However, it is still our position that the way to improve the safety performance of the railroad is not to appoint a royal commission, as the hon. member for Rimouski has suggested.
As the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Goodale) has pointed out, royal commissions take a long time to prepare their reports, and their recommendations are seldom implemented. When they are included in legislation or regulations, which is a rare occurrence, this usually happens some years after a report is brought down. No, I do not think a royal commission would expedite what the hon. member is suggesting in his motion, which reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should study the advisability of establishing a royal commission on the notable shortcomings of the Canadian railways and in particular of CNR to increase the protection of the public in general and that of the employees in
particular and to eliminate accidents and derailments of freight or passenger trains.
Rather than wait for lengthy reports and studies, it is our view that specific and immediate steps must take place to improve safety on the railways. The key channel to which such improvements can be made is, of course, the Railway Safety Advisory Committee.
The committee's most recent progress report contains several specific decisions made with respect to resolving the difficulties related to rail accidents. It has, for example, established an improved system of disclosures of accident information to the Canadian Transport Commission for analysis and action. All railway accidents are now reported directly to the Canadian Transport Commission which is responsible for follow-up investigations and for public reporting. A "tighten-up" program with regard to the fitness of operating employees reporting for duty a result of CTC order 20191-is proving effective. This involves stricter surveillance procedures by supervisors whose responsibility it is to ensure that operating employees on duty are fit, able, and alert.
A signal training program has been developed for signal construction, maintenance and operating personnel. Through on the job training, classroom instruction and home study, the program covers many areas, from general knowledge of train operation and railway signalling to studies of specific topics such as track circuits and railway highway crossing protection circuits. Employees must pass both written and practical examinations.
Minimum track standards and standards for operating rights of way are being developed. A special subcommittee was established to this end. They have to date defined specific priorities and have the agreement of Canadian Pacific Railway and Canadian National Railways to submit standards to accomplish these priorities. The CTC will also carry out research and furnish draft standards. A study for test rules improvement and signal inspection is also under way.
This is the type of positive action that is necessary. We do not need more studies or a royal commission. We need to move on the studies that have already been made. In fact preliminary figures supplied by the major railways for 1975 show to date an improvement over 1974 statistics. Crossing accidents continue to be the most serious problem. Money and research are continually going into development construction of better signal and protective devices for the safety and convenience of the public at level crossings.
The accident level to date is about the same level as in 1973 The very fact, however, that statistics do exist indicates that steps must be taken to ensure safety on the railways We must ensure that the good working relationship between the Railway Safety Advisory Committee, which includes the unions, and the CTC and MOT officials continues, and that improvements in railway safety continue to be the result.
The Canadian Railway Labour Association is also actively interested in the work and suggestions of the Railway Safety Advisory Committee. The priority matters they have indicated for the committee's working groups include the construction, maintenance and inspection of track standards; a revision of the air brake inspection and

October 24, 1975

maintenance rules; the development of a uniform code of operating rules; and regulations governing minimum training standards for those railway employees whom the RTC has designated as having duties which affect safety in the movement of trains. The hon. member for Rimouski has brought up that matter in the past. The union has also asked for a review and updating of the RTC operations, engineering and general orders, and for a review of the sections of the Railway Act having to do with the safety of operation.
I might draw to hon. members' attention the on-going improvements that are being made in the CN system as a result of maintenance, installation of new facilities, and research. New rail is being installed, and a lot of work is being done in northern Ontario and in the western provinces. In order to improve safety and capacity, CN is installing new signalling and communication facilities. Radio communications continue to be improved. As well as being active in its own search for new and improved techniques and solutions to its operating problems, it is involved in joint programs to these ends with the Department of Transport and CPR.

I support the intent and principle of the motion, except that I believe we now have the necessary procedures in operation. We have only to ensure that they are working. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to enter into the debate on the motion moved by the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard) with regard to the shortcomings of the Canadian railways. I welcome this because for many years I have been involved in the frustration of trying to deal with the freight rates of the Canadian railways, especially in the interior of British Columbia, whether it be in the south central interior or the northern interior.
One of the reasons why we are debating a motion that we should have a royal commission is that there is a lack of direction coming from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), from his office, and from the federal government. This has been especially noticeable since I have been here, which now has been three years. We know that the minister came in, threw up his hands and said that the government did not have a transportation policy. It would not be difficult to deduce from that that the railways are not paying any attention to the Minister of Transport, his
Railways Safety
department, or the federal government, and that there is really no control.
Who is running Canada, the railways or the federal government? When we consider freight rates, especially in my area, and try to understand them or to be even remotely familiar with them, we have great difficulty because the Department of Transport is very complex.
It is not difficult to understand that over the years the railways have been taking whatever the traffic will bear, especially when there is little competition. Between my riding and Vancouver there was a time when there was no competition, and it was very costly to send our apples and soft fruits to Vancouver. Then there was a highway built connecting my riding and Vancouver, and there was competition from trucking. However, it was not very long until the large railway companies were able to buy out the major truck organizations, and then the competition was more or less stunted.
We gained much experience in hauling our produce into the United States, putting it on a railway car in the United States, shipping to a point south of Regina and Assiniboia, unloading the car, putting it back on to a truck and taking it to Regina. That was cheaper than sending it by a Canadian railway. I notice that the hon. member for Coast-Chilcotin Mr. Pearsall is paying a great deal of attention to what I am saying, and what I am saying is factual.
We were at one time able to bring about competition, and then we were able to come to an agreement with the railways to have a competitive price. I remember that at one time we could load a can of apples in Kelowna, send it to Winnipeg, take it off the car, put it in cold storage, take it out of cold storage, put it back on to a car, ship it to Florida and obtain a rebate on our freight rates.
Hon. members may wonder why I am citing these examples of what used to happen. I am doing so because it is happening again today. One can send a box of apples from Washington state, which is just south of the Okanagan valley, into the eastern markets of Toronto and Montreal for 43 cents a box less than one can from Kelowna to the same markets on Canadian railways.

subtopic: SUGGESTED ROYAL COMMISSION STUDY TO IMPROVE SAFETY OF PASSENGERS AND EMPLOYEES
speechtext: Shame!

subtopic: SUGGESTED ROYAL COMMISSION STUDY TO IMPROVE SAFETY OF PASSENGERS AND EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
We are asked to buy Canadian. We are considering an advertising program in Canada to promote the sale of Canadian apples, but how on earth are we to compete with this kind of competition, which is mainly generated by our own railways, when they demand and take more money than competitive lines in the United States to haul the produce of Canada from one area to the other? Forty-three cents a box may not sound like very much money to hon. members, but it is a lot of money to the producer. The person who must absorb this amount of money is the producer. No one takes any less in Canada, and it goes right back to the producer. He has to take less for his product.
I used the examples of apples and produce, but those are not the only commodities involved in the interior of British Columbia. Commodities can be shipped from eastern Canada to Vancouver and then into Prince George for less than it can be done on a direct line which runs from Edmonton to Prince George. Someone must explain why

October 24, 1975
Railways Safety
these things happen. The ordinary layman does not have the opportunity to find out. The Department of Transport throws its hands up and says transportation policy is a mess. The department does nothing. It is time there was a royal commission.
Imagine the advantage the railways in Canada are taking with their freight rates. It does not cost the railways any more to ship commodities to these interior points, and it is not more difficult to do so. It is not any farther, but this happens because of some philosophy that it is competitive. Is this the way we are to build Canada? This is the way we have been trying to build Canada. This is the way we have been trying to have secondary industry, and this is one of the reasons why we are drawers of water. We do not have a transportation system which gives us the opportunity to compete within the framework of Canada itself. You can find all kinds of examples in Ontario especially. In Coast Chilcotin and the Prince George area many job opportunities have been lost because plants have closed.
In my riding in the interior of British Columbia a company got an area intensive grant from the federal government through DREE and established a plant which was competitive in every way. Their product was good, but they found that a large part of their market was in eastern Canada. Gf course we know that is where the population is, and we know we get discriminated against in many instances.
Because of the change in freight rates last jear this company could not compete with the American markets and so lost business. There was a stipulation that they must have so many pounds per car of a certain type of product, and so on, yet the COMINCO smelter at Trail, which is a subsidiary of the railway, was charged less. The company I speak of did not get the lesser rate because it was too small and it is not a subsidiary of the railway. There was a danger that they would have to go out of business and the DREE moneys would be lost, but luckily the market improved and they were able to pay the extra freight. They are at the mercy of these freight rates set by the railways who do not worry if somebody loses a job or goes out of business.
The former minister of transport said the department is in a mess, but we have a new minister now and I wish him well. He has a parliamentary secretary who has the interests of western Canadians at heart, but I do not think either he or the minister can do too much because they belong to a government that is not strong enough to bring the railways into line. They do not want to do it, they do not have the strength to do it, and I do not believe they are able to do it. In my opinion the motion of the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard) is a good one and I hope the government will support it.

subtopic: SUGGESTED ROYAL COMMISSION STUDY TO IMPROVE SAFETY OF PASSENGERS AND EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to take a few minutes to support the motion of my colleague from Rimouski (Mr. Allard) concerning the establishment of a royal commission on railways. If I remember correctly, Madam Speaker, on January 4, 1974, the hon. member for Rimouski requested the unanimous

consent of the House under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to discuss this motion.
As usual, his motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43 did not receive the unanimous consent of the House. In spite of this, he noted with great pleasure that March 21 of the same year was set aside for the long hoped for railway improvement study. Taking the first opportunity to urge again the government to try and find answers in order to reduce the number of railway accidents, especially in view of the many derailments in the last few years, the hon. member for Rimouski even suggested that a royal inquiry be made on the railway administrations in an attempt to solve the problems caused by the shocking deterioration of this vital and nationally important service as soon as possible. Unfortunately, the matter was forgotten as soon as it was raised. However, my colleague for Rimouski made a fresh attempt on October 28 of the same year by asking-as I have done many times with regard to the railway service in the Saguenay Lac-Saint-Jean area that an inquiry be made into the activities of the national railways.
Once again, I should like to ask all the hon. members who are here this afternoon to listen very carefully to what I will say during the few minutes allotted to me, so that I may state the reasons for my request and for supporting my colleague from Rimouski. Undoubtedly, Madam Speaker, the main reason for this request is that, as the member for Roberval, I have been aware throughout the years of many railway accidents, including derailments. In addition to those in my own riding, I could mention those which occurred in the riding of one of my colleagues from the Eastern Townships, in the province of Quebec. I intend to deal with the accidents in the passenger and freight transport services, without omitting necessarily all those which may have occurred throughout Canada.
I feel therefore it is my duty to ask again the House of Commons to set up a royal board of inquiry into the administration of our national railways, an inquiry which would certainly come up with adequate means to patch the many faults which now exist in this service of prime necessity and public interest.
In spite of all the studies which have been carried out to date, Madam Speaker, I am still convinced that such a royal board of inquiry is necessary, for such an inquiry, as I see it, would recognize the need to provide more safety and protection to passengers and railway workers alike.
At present I consider that the Transport and Communication Committee of the Canadian Transport Commission did not put enough emphasis on the inadequacies of the security standards set out in the railway area.
Referring to the report released following the 1970 general survey of railway tracks and prepared by the railway transport committee on can read the following on the first page of appendix 3:
The number of derailments in 1972 caused by the condition of Canadian National and Canadian Pacific tracks tripled since 1969, and nearly doubled since 1970.
It is easy to verify that the situation is not that bright because if one refers tothe 1959 figures one sees that there were 40 derailments, 69 in 1969, and 132 in 1972. That gives
October 24, 1975

an average increase for the three years of 90 per cent. What a shame!
I continue quoting from the same report:
Because of that continued increase in derailments it must be concluded that in a near future the number of derailments caused by the condition of the track will continue to increase as will the number of dead and wounded unless immediate steps are taken.
And those immediate steps would be to set up a serious royal inquiry that would no doubt enlighten us about the faults of the present administration and bring in corrective measures.
It is very important to know how to distinguish between accidental and localized administrative faults which can be corrected on the spot, and structural, basic faults which would require a complete overhaul of the organizations involved. So, Madam Speaker, this is a matter of momentous importance which deserves all our attention and all our energy if we want to get in line with current and future requirements and restore to our railways their reputation of yesteryear which was recognized throughout the whole world. Because we know that for a long time our railway were the pride of Canadians, financiers, administrators, employees and all the external traffic. But today, instead of boasting a futuristic railway network we make do with a very poor system. We were unable to maintain our railroads and the rolling stock. I should like to quote some examples of derailments that occurred, mainly in Quebec as I cannot mention all the derailments that were reported throughout the country. I should draw to your attention several derailments that occurred in my area last year, about 70 miles from Mont-Joli and more precisely in Routhierville, where about twenty cars loaded with oil and several other goods ran off the line. There was also another derailment within the same year between Mont-Joli and Rimouski, several cars loaded with passengers. Fortunately there was no fatality but it was a pity to see so much material damages. And I remember the accident I already mentioned to this House: between Montreal and Chambord during the winter a train with almost 100 passengers left the tracks at three o'clock in the morning. The passengers had to stay in the train without anything to eat and I had to phone Montreal to get the authorization to give some food to those people and to call for buses that arrived only at two o'clock in the afternoon. Can you imagine all those people waiting in the train? Madam Speaker, when such derailments happen the passengers are not ready to take another CN train the day after. They always say never again!
Madam Speaker, the accidents I just mentioned are rather important. And in the long term, they are vey costly if you consider the large number of derailments in Canada in recent years.
Finally, hon. members will agree that if the Canadian Transport Commission has found it wise to recommend to the Canadian National Railways to reduce the speed of passenger trains to 40 miles an hour, and often to 20 to 25 miles an hour, all year long yet, it was to bring down as much as possible the number of accidents on their railways.
I can then say that this coincides perfectly with the aim of this motion, which is simply to find serious solutions to that great number of derailments. For I remember that not
Railways Safety
so long ago, derailments could be counted on the fingers of one hand, whereas now they can hardly be counted with a calculating machine.
No doubt, Madam Speaker, accidents used to be less frequent, quite simply because tracks were well-maintained. In fact, for every seven miles of railway tracks, there were four employees responsible for maintaining and looking after those tracks.
Moreover, tracks were inspected everyday and frequently after the passing of passenger or freight trains. It has now been thought wise to increase sections to about 20 miles, while at the same time reducing the number of personnel in charge of the maintenance and surveillance of those tracks.
Funniest of all about railroad inspection, employees and maintenance crews most of the time travel the section they are in charge of by car on the highway. And they claim they have inspected railway tracks. I would rather say they go for a Sunday drive.
Madam Speaker, it is my sincere belief that utter mismanagement of the Canadian National results in undue expenses and shameful waste.
Think also of CN senior executives who are provided with company cars and credit cards with unlimited coverage. I think I am justified in requesting in my own name and in the name of my colleague, with respect to the activities of the national railways, the institution of the famous royal inquiry commission.
Before concluding, Madam Speaker, I wish to remark that before engaging into secondary ventures as the building of towers, the development of shopping centres and real estate such as luxury hotels, our railways should first give an assurance they will adequately maintain facilities and services and also, since we are on this matter, keep a large number of cars and locomotives in railway service.
Let me speak of what happens and the noise that surrounds the trains. Doing repair work in a milk car, which is very often the case, on the heating system that is always out of service or the brakes that do not work most of the time, it is very complicated matter. Repairs used to be done locally. In Chambord, there was a repair shop. But today, if a button does not work, if there is a power failure, if there is no heating in some car, the latter must be sent to Montreal for repair.
In the meantime everybody gets cold in the train, and that is the kind of service we are getting in our trains. For this reason, I am pleased to support the motion of my colleague, and I hope the government will take good note and attempt to give the CN the men or technicians needed to guarantee better service to the people.

speechtext:
Many people in my area, as well as members from my area, saw the railways fold up their cabooses and all other facilities about five or six years ago. They simply removed them from my area. It might be very proper for those who have passenger trains to talk about them and their safety. However, we do not even have passenger trains.

I feel that asking for a royal commission, as my colleague has stated, will not result soon enough in specific and decisive action which is required to ensure safety on our railway system or to improve the very poor system we have at the present time.
In addition, a royal commission at this time would cost $1 million, $2 million or $3 million. What is the price of a royal commission? What is the length of time it will be in effect? subtopic: SUGGESTED ROYAL COMMISSION STUDY TO IMPROVE SAFETY OF PASSENGERS AND EMPLOYEES

Let us wait and see what will happen with our new Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang). I believe he is a sincere person, one who will do his level best to ensure that Canada has the best type of freight or passenger service, whether it is by air or water. If we get a train in Wiarton, I will invite the hon. member to be the second man on, because I am going to be the first!
One member spoke earlier about the respect and admiration the railways had at one time. I agree that at one time the railways did hold the respect and esteem of people right across this country. speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: SUGGESTED ROYAL COMMISSION STUDY TO IMPROVE SAFETY OF PASSENGERS AND EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
I do not think that a royal commission will bring back that respect. It is something that has to be undertaken by the railways, Canadian National, Canadian Pacific, and every man Jack that works for them. They are the people who provide the service and the safety.
I am sure that every member who represents a rural area has received complaints from farmers in his area about bush and brush growing along the sides of railway tracks. This is not cut back. Therefore people driving along our highways and byways cannot see when a train is approaching. There have been numerous instances in my area, particularly since the beginning of the oil train runs from Montreal to the Douglas Point nuclear power development, of trains travelling late at night and early into the morning. People have driven right up to these railways crossings only to find suddenly there is a train on them. They cannot see far enough down the track to have an
adequate stopping distance when traffic is on the line. The railways could rectify this by simply getting the crews out to clear the brush, fences, and waste that are piling up along the rights of way. I am not sure this will come about even with a royal commission, but members of parliament must let the railways know the feelings of the people they represent.
With regard to the runs from Montreal which carry bunker oil to the nuclear power station, I was surprised to find that the railways supply the lines and the engines, but somebody else supplies the cars. I have been successful with regard to having the oil cars marked. When I tried to pursue this further as to who was responsible, I found out that it was not the railways that are responsible for marking the cars, but those who own them. You must go through a devious route to find out who owns the cars and who is responsible for marking them. This is something the safety people should look into.
There should be better illumination of the markings, particularly on the black oil cars that travel the width and breadth of this country, so that during the dark hours those approaching a crossing will have their lights reflected and know that there is a moving obstacle. In many cases people have driven right into the side of a moving car.
I think that positive steps are being taken by the railway safety advisory committee, and this is the route we should continue to follow. The Ministry of Transport, however, sees the railway safety matter as necessitating a multi-faceted program of which this committee is one part. We are thus presently pursuing many other programs which will lead to the improvement of safety on the railways.
It is on these other programs that I wish to take a few minutes to elaborate. There is the transportation policy on rail system development and financing. The transport policy which is now being prepared for legislation provides for ongoing financing to ensure that a viable railway system is available for Canadian transportation.
We in this House talk about the improvements we would like to see. We talk about brushing, a new road system, overpasses, underpasses, and tunnels. However, we must realize that this is going to cost money. The money must be provided for this type of safety endeavour before it can be put into effect.
The program will ensure that ongoing financing is available to that sector. This naturally provides for a high level of maintenance which leads to improved safety of operations. The Hall and Snavely Commissions are assisting us in our program on the whole matter of grain transport with the objective of providing a high quality rail transportation system.
Many people travel throughout the world and see a number of different railway systems in Europe and in England from which we can learn many things. I also think we can learn of some of the pitfalls and problems.
Often not enough consideration is given to railways in rural areas. I think members from rural areas will back me up in that. People used to see the 9.20 train going through at 9.20 in the morning and returning at 8.30 at night. The action really started when the railways stopped running

October 24, 1975

on time. People in the area knew when the train went through, and then they started running late and everyone became confused. The first thing you knew was that people along the track thought the 9.20 had gone through, perhaps they could not see down the right of way as far as they should, and the next thing is it is 9.45 and they are hit.

subtopic: SUGGESTED ROYAL COMMISSION STUDY TO IMPROVE SAFETY OF PASSENGERS AND EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Well let us talk about roadbeds for a moment. Anyone who was present near the end of the transport meetings last year will certainly have seen some of the roadbeds in western Canada and in eastern Canada which need upgrading and which are not fit for the type of traffic they are expected to carry. Let us do something about them, but setting up a royal commission which might take three years to report is not going to do much to solve the problem right now.
Purchase of railway cars for grain is also something we can talk about, as well as grain transportation generally. The government has either ordered or purchased 4,000 covered hopper cars for the transportation of grain. This, in addition to providing capacity for the movement of grain, I believe leads to a safer operation in grain transportation. Any kind of operation that must be speedy leads to danger somewhere along the route. The covered hopper cars are easily loaded at the elevators and unloaded at the terminals without the use of shovels, grain doors and so on, and they certainly upgrade the system.
In addition to this improved safety factor by the terminal operators, there is a rail operational consideration whereby these cars lead to the displacement of some of the obsolete boxcar type of equipment. One covered hopper car replaces two of these obsolete cars. The latest design provides for a much safer train and yard movement operation. I am sure many hon. members realize, if they see some of the 100 and even 200 car trains travelling through cities and across Canada, that if these trains are cut in half safety factors will be improved, whether these trains are carrying grain, oil, or any other type of material.
With regard to providing more money for capital acquisition of necessary equipment for upgrading railway lines, this to some is one of the top priorities that should be undertaken at the present time. In the analyses of CN budgets great consideration is given to the financial resources needed to ensure that CN can maintain the system they have. It may not be very good, but they do at least want to maintain what they have. This ensures that they have the capability to operate in a safe manner. Particular emphasis is placed on ensuring that railway yards and facilities receive maintenance on a regular basis
Railways Safety
and that funds are made available for the purchase of equipment to replace obsolete equipment and the maintenance of railway equipment on hand.
With regard to development of a railway monitoring system to identify specific problems and develop reasonable solutions, as an ongoing program the CNR has been making progress in the use of hot journal box detectors. At one time this was one of the primary causes of derailment and other troubles, particularly with passenger cars. These detectors can do much to assist in making rail stock safer so far as passenger and freight trains are concerned. They now have these sensing devices on main routes across Canada, as hon. members probably know. The railways are now experimenting with 24 detectors reporting to a computer via Bell telephone, and the results are so favourable that they are progressing with this program on the rest of the route and it is expected to be completed by the middle of next year. During the balance of this year they will be refined even further. The computer has been found to be much more critical and thorough in its reading of the situation than any manpower.
As for joint participation of rail capacity development, the ministry of transport is taking the lead in working with the railways to develop programs and alternatives to provide for an orderly development of rail transportation infrastructure in Canada. Through these programs we are able to ensure that new rail lines and improvements to existing routes as well as terminals are planned and developed in such a way as to give the best possible system for the funds that are applied.
Once again I want to congratulate the hon. member for Rimouski for raising this very important item this afternoon, particularly since it concerns so many of us. But I should have liked to see the matter go even further, as we must also take a look not only at rail transportation but at all facets of transportation in this country, including air and sea. We must examine every alternative so as to develop a better rail system.
I agree with what the hon. member said earlier that the development of this country has depended, during the century that we have been in existence, on our railways. It is on this type of service that we can build and make Canada a much better country for all to live in, one of which we will all be justly proud.
